messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of GLM output
parts:
Hi

Without the data in question, this is a little tricky to answer, but
these coefficients are in logits (because you use binomial for the
error family, which in turn means you have logit as the link
function). Thus, the intercept gives you the logit of the mean of the
first variable (and its level), and the coefficients that follow give
you logits of differences between means.

> 1/(1+1/(exp(3.9926)))
[1] 0.9818826

> 1/(1+1/(exp(3.9926-3.6094)))
[1] 0.5946447

The means are easier to get with this, which you might want to report
as effect sizes.

tapply(predict(NAME OF THE MODEL, type="response"), VARIABLE, mean)

As to the parameters for the variables as such, I think you will get
those from the ANOVA table for the model. Note: this will be based on
sequential sums of squares unless you change this. SPSS and other
software offers options here, too, but do not do sequential SS by
default. In R, the library(car) allows you to choose Type III sums of
squares.

HTH a little, but this is really tough stuff. The books by Michael
Crawley (2002, 2005) are rather good on these issues.
Cheers,

STG
--

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of GLM output
parts:
Hi Thomas

Well, actually I was not so happy with my response so I did a little
reading yesterday and can now clarify at least the part about the
intercept a bit:

First, the intercept: R applies dummy coding to the categorical
variables. With binary variables, this means that the alphabetically
first level is set to 0 and the other one to 1. These variable levels
are then treated as the reference levels and all coefficients that
follow indicate the change the levels bring about (where in the case
of a logistic regression the logit thing applies again). However, this
does not give you the parameter estimates for each factor.

Second, as to the factors' parameter estimates. I still think that the
answer is to get the ANOVA table. Try this

# set up a data set that might be like yours
f1<-factor(sample(c("a", "b"), 100, replace=T))
f2<-factor(sample(c("x", "y"), 100, replace=T))
y<-sample(c(0, 1), 100, replace=T)

# compute the logistic regression
model<-glm(y ~ f1+f2, family="binomial")

# look at the summary output
summary(model)

# look at the ANOVA table
anova(model)

Note that my comments from the last mail still apply: The terms are
added sequentially (as it says there!). If you don't want that:

library(car)
Anova(model, type="III", test.statistic="F") # or test.statistic="LR"
or test.statistic="Wald"

which I guess is what you want. Don't forget, however, to some model
checking ...

par(mfrow=c(2, 2))
plot(model)

HTH,

STG

Hi everyone!

First of all a big thank you to Stefan for helping me out with this
one! Now that I finally know how to get it in R, I might also be able
to explain what it was that I was after:

Stefan wondered whether I wanted the means, so he suggested:
tapply(predict(NAME OF THE MODEL, type="response"), VARIABLE, mean)

after fiddling around with that command line [not a very scientific
approach but sometimes I just have to get my hands on something to
fully understand it...], I realised that I was actually looking for
this:

tapply(predict(NAME OF THE MODEL, type="link"), VARIABLE, mean)

This gives me logit parameters for all levels of a factor, which I
then can transform to get their logistic value [e.g. as Stefan
suggested via: 1/(1+1/exp(x))].

Why would I want to do this? Well, so far I've worked with Goldvarb
with reports parameters on the logistic scale. Now when I use the
above tapply-command in R and transform the resulting parameters, I
can finally compare my Goldvarb model with the model that R comes up
with. And finally, proceeding as outlined abobe, I actually get
values similar to the ones Goldvarb reports. Yippee!

Hope I didn't bore anyone with this...

Cheers!

Thomas
